title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers are using generative AI to create deepfakes of real people, including a South Florida immigration attorney, to impersonate them on social media and in phone calls. The system failure here is not a malfunction of the AI itself but a social one: fraudsters have weaponized voice cloning and image synthesis tools to conduct impersonation at scale. Immigrants seeking legal services were targeted with fake profiles and cloned voices, losing money to non-existent legal consultations.

This deployment failure occurs at the point where AI-generated content enters the world with no authentication layer and no barrier to falsification. The tools used were not designed for fraud but were repurposed by bad actors. Catching this would require either AI vendors implementing detection methods on their platforms, social media providers verifying professional identities, or targets being trained to verify people through channels independent of the initial contact.

It is not established whether the scammers who created these deepfakes faced any legal consequences or whether any particular AI tool was identified as the source.

summary:
# Summary

Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used by scammers to steal millions of dollars by creating convincing deepfakes of voices, photos, and phone calls. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report found that Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice was cloned to target immigrants and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia had 71 complaints totaling over $10.4 million.

Scammers are using generative AI to clone voices from social media, spoof phone numbers, create fake photographs, and research personal relationships to make scams more believable. The "AI grandparent scam" is a growing trend where criminals impersonate relatives claiming to need urgent money. Federal investigators warn that as AI tools become cheaper and more accessible, these scams will continue evolving. Authorities recommend establishing secret code words with family members, verifying requests through known phone numbers, and never sending money based on unexpected calls or emails.
